title: The Bittersweet Lesson of Scaling in AI for Materials
content: Abstract: AI has the potential to bring much-needed acceleration to the development of chemicals and materials for energy and sustainability, just like it has delivered intelligence gains in other fields. The path to success goes through scaling, perhaps exclusively through scaling. Rich Sutton’s ‘bitter lesson’ states that “general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective” in AI. The corollaries are bittersweet in chemistry and materials.
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract : AI has the potential to bring much-needed acceleration to the development of chemicals and materials for energy and sustainability, just like it has delivered intelligence gains in other fields. The path to success goes through scaling, perhaps exclusively through scaling. Rich Sutton's 'bitter lesson' states that "general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective" in AI. The corollaries are bittersweet in chemistry and materials. The lesson permeates through the use of AI in chemistry and materials. The tremendous success of universal ML interatomic potentials (MLIPs) as surrogate for quantum-mechanical energies and forces is unarguable. Trained on 100-million-count datasets, they reflect scaling laws similar to the ones in language or vision models, generalizing to new scientific questions and enabling simulations that were intractable a few years ago. Generative models, trained mostly on the same synthetic data, are currently being used to propose novel materials at machine speed. The discussion around the power of inductive bias (energy conservation, equivariance) and whether it is better reflected in model architecture or in training strategy is very much ongoing. The physical sciences may well be the last holdout for domain knowledge and inductive bias, or maybe they will ultimately follow the same trends as other domains. But MLIPs are surrogates for physics-based simulators, and arguably, materials only truly matter if they are made in the lab and then scaled up industrially and commercially. This is the truly bitter scaling lesson in materials. The promise of AI for chemistry and materials needs to be realized through very traditional, expensive and slow channels. In this talk, I will describe our group's work both in the highly scalable fusion of simulations and machine learning, and in the "high-contact" and lower throughput effort of translating AI designs into tangible, scalable products, in areas like heterogeneous catalysis, battery materials or sustainable polymers Bio: Rafael Gomez-Bombarelli is the Paul M Cook Associate Professor in MIT's Department of Materials Science and Engineering; and co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer at Lila Sciences. He earned his undergraduate and graduate degrees in chemistry from the University of Salamanca, Spain, and conducted postdoctoral research at Heriot-Watt University and Harvard University, under Alan Aspuru-Guzik. Rafa's research integrates machine learning with atomistic simulations to expedite the discovery and design of novel materials for applications in energy, sustainability, and healthcare.
summaryRaw: The Bittersweet Lesson of Scaling in AI for Materials

title: Test-Time Scaling Makes Overtraining Compute-Optimal
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract Modern LLMs scale at test-time, e.g. via repeated sampling, where inference cost grows with model size and the number of samples. This creates a trade-off that pretraining scaling laws, such as Chinchilla, do not address. In this talk, we present Train-to-Test (T^2) scaling laws that jointly optimize model size, training tokens, and number of inference samples under fixed end-to-end budgets. T^2 modernizes pretraining scaling laws with pass@k modeling used for test-time scaling, then jointly optimizes pretraining and test-time decisions. Forecasts from T^2 are robust over distinct modeling approaches: measuring joint scaling effect on the task loss and modeling impact on task accuracy. Across eight downstream tasks, we find that when accounting for inference cost, optimal pretraining decisions shift radically into the overtraining regime, well-outside of the range of standard pretraining scaling suites. We validate our results by pretraining heavily overtrained models in the optimal region that T^2 scaling forecasts, confirming their substantially stronger performance compared to pretraining scaling alone. Finally, as frontier LLMs are post-trained, we show that our findings survive the post-training stage, making T^2 scaling meaningful in modern deployments. Link to Bio: https://nick11roberts.science/ Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series

title: Do Thinking Tokens Help with Safety?
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract : Today's reasoning models use thinking tokens to attain stronger performance on benchmarks than their instruction-tuned counterparts. It is also generally believed that this more "deliberative" mode should improve alignment and safety, by providing the model a safe space to consider whether its planned answer to a request violates its safety principles. We present evidence that this intuition is not always correct. Across frontier open-weight reasoning models spanning GPT-OSS, Qwen, Olmo, and Phi families, we find that the eventual refusal/compliance outcome is already strongly predictable via a trained head on the first token's hidden representation (0.84-0.95 AUROC and ∼88% balanced accuracy for predicting refusal/compliance) before any visible thinking. The thinking process turns out to be more akin to prefix completion than to deliberative revision, with the final outcome rarely changing after the first ∼20% of thinking, despite giving the appearance of deliberation at the text level (∼74% of text-level deliberations occur when the response distribution is already locked to one refusal/compliance side). We also find that existing inference-time and training-based safety interventions, despite being motivated by the goal of inducing deliberation, largely shift model behavior toward over-refusal while suppressing already-scarce deliberation signals. Our results suggest that safety behavior in current reasoning models is much less deliberative than commonly assumed, and highlight the need for methods that induce real safety deliberation. Bio : Narutatsu Ri is a second-year Ph.D. student advised by Professor Sanjeev Arora. His research focuses on the safety and alignment of large foundation models, with particular interests in measuring and mitigating misalignment, scalable oversight, and the safety implications of self-improving AI systems. Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series

title: Synthetic Data, Real Benefits: Reliable Inference and Principled Model Steering
rawEventDetails: Speaker Yaniv Romano Affiliation Technion- Israel Institute of Technology Details Event Description Abstract AI models are powerful, yet their use in practice raises two fundamental challenges. The first is trust: how can we make reliable inferences from black-box models when we only have a few reference examples to rely on? The second is steerability: how can we guide AI generation when we can recognize the outputs we prefer but cannot precisely quantify our preferences? In this talk, I will show how statistics and AI can empower one another to tackle both challenges. The first part focuses on reliable inference under limited data. I'll introduce General Synthetic-Powered Inference (GESPI), a framework that safely enhances the sample efficiency of any statistical inference procedure—such as conformal prediction and hypothesis testing—by adaptively leveraging synthetic data. GESPI provides distribution-free error control regardless of synthetic-data quality while improving utility when those data are informative. I'll demonstrate its applicability across domains ranging from predictive uncertainty quantification to principled win-rate evaluation of large reasoning models. I'll also discuss how these ideas can support large-scale scientific discovery with false discovery rate control. In the second part, I'll introduce Preference-based Metropolis-Hastings (Pref-MH): a model-steering framework that leverages pairwise votes from an LLM judge to generate data satisfying complex properties of interest. Pref-MH exploits a novel connection between MH and the Bradley-Terry preference model. This connection enables rigorous steering of a base AI generator toward a target distribution that favors outputs preferred by the judge, without ever needing to estimate the judge's latent reward. Finally, I'll demonstrate Pref-MH in molecular design and show how the resulting synthetic data improve downstream inference when incorporated into GESPI. Bio Yaniv Romano is an associate professor in the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering and Computer Science at the Technion. He is also affiliated with NVIDIA as a visiting professor. Previously, he was a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Statistics at Stanford University. Yaniv holds a PhD, an MSc, and a BSc in electrical engineering, all from the Technion. His super-resolution technology, invented with Peyman Milanfar, has been integrated into Google’s flagship products, including Pixel phones. His uncertainty quantification method, developed with Emmanuel Candès, was used by The Washington Post to estimate outstanding votes during the U.S. presidential election. Yaniv has received several honors and awards, including an ERC Starting Grant, the SIAG/IS Early Career Prize, the Sheila Samson Prime Minister’s Prize (Researcher Recruitment Prize), the IEEE Signal Processing Society Best Paper Award, the Alon Scholarship, the Krill Prize for Excellence in Scientific Research, and the Henry Taub Prize for Academic Excellence. Yaniv is a member of the Young Israel Academy. This seminar is supported with funds from the Korhammer Lecture Series. Sponsors Guillermo Sapiro Pramod Viswanath Contact Ryann Myers [email protected]

title: Princeton University Robotics Seminar
rawEventDetails: Speaker Maurizio Porfiri Affiliation New York University Details Event Description Abstract: How and why base vibration can stabilize an inverted pendulum has puzzled the scientific community for decades, until Pyotr Kapitza's work on dynamic stabilization pointed to the alternation between unstable and stable modes as a pathway to stability. We report the discovery of a mechanical oscillator that switches between two unstable modes, has an unstable average, and yet can be dynamically stabilized. Our impossible system is governed by a modified Meissner’s model – a one-degree-of-freedom oscillator where both stiffness and damping are modulated through a square wave to switch between positive and negative values. We study the system through the lens of the theory of oscillations in a rapidly oscillating field by Landau and Lifshitz, providing insights into the physical underpinnings of “dynamic stabilization 2.0”. We validate the theory's predictions by computing Floquet exponents, yielding exact results on the emergence and topology of compact antiresonance windows where the system is stable. We provide experimental evidence of the feasibility of this new form of dynamic stabilization through a “Frankenstein” oscillator developed at Stony Brook University in collaboration with Prof. Paolo Celli and his student, David Xiedeng. The oscillator comprises a cantilever beam subject to magnetic and aerodynamic forcing, modulated in time to alternate between unstable configurations and retain an unstable mean. The prospect of dynamic stabilization in the absence of any stable feature has vast implications for network dynamical systems, structural mechanics, and robotics. Bio: Maurizio Porfiri is an Institute Professor at New York University Tandon School of Engineering (Departments of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Biomedical Engineering, Center for Urban Science and Progress, CUSP, and Civil and Urban Engineering). He is presently the Director of CUSP and the founding Director of the Urban Institute. He received M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees in Engineering Mechanics from Virginia Tech; a “Laurea” in Electrical Engineering and a Ph.D. in Theoretical and Applied Mechanics from Sapienza University of Rome and the University of Toulon. He conducts and supervises research on complex systems, with applications ranging from mechanics and robotics to urban science and behavioral biology. This seminar is supported with funds from the Korhammer Lecture Series.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Speaker: Taylor Webb, Department of Psychology, Princeton University Talk Abstract: There is a longstanding tension in cognitive science between theories that emphasize the structured, symbolic aspects of the mind — drawing an analogy to traditional computer programs — and the emergent properties of cognition that seem to be better explained by neural networks. The rise of AI systems that are powered by neural networks, but that display many of the properties associated with symbolic cognitive models (e.g., compositionality, reasoning) has reinvigorated this debate, while leaving open the question of how these systems achieve the capabilities that were thought to require innate symbol processing, and what this says about the mechanistic basis of those capabilities in human cognition. In this talk, I will argue that symbol-like behavioral capabilities in modern neural networks are supported by an emergent form of symbolic computation, and illustrate how this is implemented by their internal mechanisms. I will also discuss the factors that lead to the emergence of these mechanisms, and will consider a case that illustrates how symbolic mechanisms are not necessarily human-like. Overall, these results suggest that connectionist principles may be sufficient to account for the symbol-like aspects of human cognition, while also illustrating how symbolic cognitive models can be translated into mechanistic theories.

title: DARK MANSIONS: AI, Innovation, and Fermat’s Last Theorem
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Yiu, Kosoy, and Gopnik (2024) argue that “Cultural evolution depends on a fine balance between imitation and innovation.” Writing in a world prior to reasoning models, they argued that large language models fall squarely on the imitation side. This paper—focused principally on formal and scientific innovation—proposes a finer-grained, three-tier taxonomy: Tier 1 is transmission, Tier 2 is something new (invention) within a fixed problem formulation, and Tier 3 is framework-generating innovation. Tier 3 requires both historical novelty—a new construction or framework—and functional novelty—a downstream dividend, where the apparatus introduced to solve a problem helps to reorganize later work. We explore Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem as a case of Tier 3 innovation. Core elements of the proof architecture—especially the R = T modularity-lifting strategy and Taylor–Wiles patching—were not present in the prior mathematical literature. Moreover, the proof apparatus has had substantial downstream impact on number theory and the Langlands program. We consider whether a current frontier AI system trained on pre‑1987 mathematical sources could have produced a Wiles-type proof strategy, and offer reasons for doubt. Broadening the argument beyond the Wiles proof, we analyze three current AI paradigms for AI in mathematics and argue that they do not yet offer clear mechanisms for Tier 3 innovation. We then assess the empirical record of AI-assisted mathematical discovery, including the refutation of the unit-distance conjecture and the proof of the existence of non-sofic groups. We find a growing number of striking Tier 2 achievements, but no evidence yet of Tier 3 innovation. Tier 3 innovation, we propose, depends on three capacities—imagination, judgment, and tenacity, understood functionally as capacities for novel decomposition, structural evaluation, and sustained exploration. Current architectures have not shown these capacities at the scale required for Tier 3 innovation. The paper concludes with reflections on the architectural changes that may be needed for the innovation that comes from what Andrew Wiles vividly describes as stumbling around in “dark mansions.” Bio: Joshua Cohen is a political philosopher. He has written on issues of democratic theory, freedom of expression, religious freedom, political equality, democracy and digital technology, good jobs, and global justice. His books include On Democracy (with Joel Rogers); Democracy and Associations ( with Joel Rogers); Philosophy, Politics, Democracy ; Rousseau: A Free Community of Equals ; and The Arc of the Moral Universe and Other Essays . He is co-editor of the Norton Introduction to Philosophy , now in its third edition. Cohen taught at MIT (1977-2005), Stanford (2005-2014), is currently on the faculty at Apple University, and is Distinguished Senior Fellow in Law, Philosophy, and Political Science at University of California, Berkeley. Cohen held the Romanell-Phi Beta Kappa Professorship in 2002-3; gave the Tanner Lectures at UC Berkeley in 2007; the Comte Lectures at LSE in 2012; and the Annual Lecture on Ethics and AI at Oxford in 2024. He is co-editor-in-chief of Boston Review . This talk will be recorded and livestreamed. The recording will be posted to the CITP website, the CITP YouTube channel and the University Media Central channel. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Instructor: Christopher Kenny, Postdoctoral Research Associate, Data-Driven Social Science This workshop introduces researchers to AI coding agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, as tools for research assistance in the social sciences. These agents work directly inside a project, editing files and running code, in ways that raise the same reliability questions as a human research assistant. A well-structured project can keep an agent's work inspectable through version control, written instructions, and automated checks that separate unreviewed from human-approved work. I will demonstrate structuring a project this way, with a short discussion of common failure points and the practices that catch them before they reach a final product. By the end, attendees will be able to set up a project for agent-assisted research and be comfortable applying best practices for instructing, validating, and reviewing an agent's work.
